# {{title}}

The objective this serves, in one sentence, with a link to the idea that holds it. An experiment that cannot name what it is in service of has nothing to be measured against.

The `branch` above is the **idea's**, not this experiment's: every experiment under one objective works on one branch, so the second spike can start from what the first one left.

## Unknowns it clears

Which of the idea's unknowns this goes after, quoted so the note is readable on its own. Anything it will not touch stays on the idea and waits for another experiment. Going after all of them at once is the usual way to clear none of them.

## Experiment

What gets built, and (just as important) what it deliberately fakes. Everything the unknowns do not touch is hardcoded.

If the way the experiment is being run changes partway, record that here, dated, **before running the changed version**. A protocol change written down afterwards is indistinguishable from a rationalisation.

## Acceptance criteria

What we would call a successful experiment, written now, before any of it exists.

Observable outcomes rather than impressions: nothing here has to be a number, but it has to be something a person could point at and agree on without having been in the room. "It works well" is not a criterion; "the panel shows which layer a thing attached to" is. Say what an unsuccessful one looks like too, when that is not simply the absence of the above.

Where the real subject cannot exercise one of these, say so and pre-register the synthetic case that will, kept separate from the judgment made against real material, so nobody later reads the two as the same evidence.

Say what would count as enough to judge on, so stopping is a decision someone can make rather than a feeling.

## Findings

Dated entries, appended while running. Write them as they happen rather than reconstructing them afterwards, and record the things you expected to find that did not turn up: those are the entries that change your mind later.

Title each entry with the claim it makes rather than the topic it covers: "the boundary sits further out than assumed" is worth more than "extraction results".

### {{date:YYYY-MM-DD}}

## Conclusion

What the unknowns turned out to be, stated so the learning **generalises beyond this one case**, and **how far the evidence actually reaches**: how many inputs, how many people, on whose machine. That scope sentence carries real weight; one person on one case is a narrow base, and saying so is what stops the result being over-trusted a year from now.

Name the confounds rather than laundering them. If the same person built the thing and judged it, say so: that settles a shape and tells you nothing about whether anyone else wants it.

Then walk the criteria: which were met, which were not, and which were never judged.
